title: Semantic Debt
description_html: Software systems do not only accumulate technical debt. They accumulate semantic debt: the future cost of meaning that is underdefined, misplaced, contradictory, stale, fragmented, opaque, overcoupled, overclaimed, inadmissible, or only recoverable through inference. Technical debt concerns the burden created by implementation shortcuts, architectural compromises, postponed refactoring, or quality degradation. Semantic debt concerns a different layer: the decay of recoverable meaning. A system may compile, pass tests, and remain operational while its terms drift, its categories collapse, its authority assumptions hide, its decisions vaporize, its evidence becomes inadmissible, and its claims outrun what its artifacts can support. This paper proposes a two-axis ontology of semantic debt. The first axis defines seven semantic subdomains: lexical debt, ontological debt, boundary debt, procedural debt, evidentiary debt, authority debt, and claim debt. The second axis defines nine debt modes: underdefinition, contradiction, fragmentation, staleness, opacity, overcoupling, inadmissibility, overclaim, and lossy translation. Together, these axes give semantic debt a coordinate system. A debt item is not merely named. It is located by what kind of meaning is failing and by how that failure manifests. The paper gives special attention to semantic fragmentation. Fragmentation is not a peer subdomain beside lexical, ontological, boundary, procedural, evidentiary, authority, and claim debt.
